title: How to Plan a Family Trip: Traveling Abroad with Kids
metaTitle: How to Plan a Family Trip: Traveling Abroad with Kids - myTravel Blog
description: A guide to planning a family trip abroad with kids. From choosing a destination and flight tips to picking accommodation and building kid-friendly itineraries, here's everything you need for family travel.
ogDescription: A guide to planning a family trip abroad with kids. From choosing a destination to kid-friendly itineraries, here's everything you need for family travel.
intro:
Traveling abroad with kids gives the whole family memories to treasure. Experiencing an unfamiliar culture together, tasting new food, and marveling at beautiful scenery side by side are the moments that deepen the bonds within a family. At the same time, traveling with children calls for thorough preparation. Things you can shrug off on an adults-only trip can turn into real problems once a child is along.

"My child is still so young—isn't a trip abroad too much?" Plenty of parents worry about exactly this. But if you choose the right destination, adjust the pace to your child's condition, and pack the essentials, a trip abroad with your child can absolutely be safe and enjoyable. This article walks you through everything about family travel abroad in detail—from how to choose a destination and flight tips to picking a place to stay, adjusting the intensity of your itinerary by age, and preparing for emergencies.

sections.h2: Choosing a Family Destination: 5 Key Criteria
sections.html:
It's no exaggeration to say that 80% of whether a family trip succeeds is decided by the choice of destination. Let's look at the five criteria you should always weigh when picking a destination that works well with kids.

1. Flight time

The right flight time depends on your child's age. If you're traveling with an infant or toddler under 3, a nearby destination within 4 hours of flying is the safe choice. Japan (2–3 hours), Taiwan (2.5 hours), major Chinese cities (2–3 hours), and the Philippines (4 hours) all fit the bill. With a child aged 4–7, flights of up to 5–6 hours are manageable. Consider Thailand (5.5 hours), Vietnam (5 hours), or Singapore (6 hours). For elementary-school age and up, long-haul flights become possible, but if it's their first time, it's better to start with destinations under 10 hours away, such as Hawaii (8 hours), Guam (4.5 hours), or Australia (9–10 hours).

2. Hygiene and medical care

Children have weaker immune systems and are sensitive to food, so it's important to choose a country with high hygiene standards. Japan, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, and developed European countries all have high standards of hygiene and well-established medical systems, so you can travel with peace of mind. Even within Southeast Asia, major cities like Singapore, Bangkok (Thailand), and Kuala Lumpur (Malaysia) have international-standard hospitals and are relatively safe. In places where you have to boil water before drinking it or where street-food hygiene is a concern, you'll need to pay extra attention to your child's meals.

3. Safety

Check the local security situation and the risk of natural disasters. Government travel-advisory websites let you check the alert level for each country. Up to the lowest advisory level, family travel is usually fine, but it's best to avoid areas rated at a "reconsider travel" level or higher. Also check whether your travel dates fall in a season prone to typhoons, monsoons, earthquakes, or other natural disasters.

4. Kid-friendly facilities

A place rich in facilities and programs your child can enjoy is well suited to family travel. Cities with plenty of attractions for children—theme parks, aquariums, zoos, water parks, children's museums—are ideal. Everyday conveniences matter too: whether restaurants offer a kids' menu, whether it's easy to get around with a stroller, and whether diaper-changing stations are available.

5. Time difference and climate

A destination with a large time difference can throw off your child's body clock significantly. If possible, a destination within 3 hours of time difference is easier to adjust to. Japan (no time difference), Southeast Asia (1–2 hours), and Australia (0–1 hours) are easy to adjust to. Europe (7–8 hours) and the U.S. East Coast (14 hours) can take 2–3 days to adjust to, so build some slack into your schedule. Climate matters too. With kids along, it's best to avoid extreme heat (over 40°C / 104°F) or cold (below -10°C / 14°F), and visiting during the dry season is more comfortable.

1. Singapore

Singapore is like a textbook example of a family destination. With a flight time of 6 hours and a 1-hour time difference, it's easy to reach, and it boasts world-class hygiene and safety. There's a genuine wealth of things for kids to do. Universal Studios Singapore, the Sentosa Island water parks, S.E.A. Aquarium, Singapore Zoo (and the Night Safari), and Gardens by the Bay—there's no shortage of places the whole family can enjoy together. Most venues are fully air-conditioned, stroller-accessible, and easy to communicate in since English is widely spoken. As a multicultural country, it's easy to find a variety of food—Korean, Japanese, Chinese—so meals that suit your child's tastes are no problem.

2. Hawaii

Hawaii is a great place to show your child the beauty of nature. It's a long haul at about 8 hours of flight time, but direct flights let you get there without a layover. Waikiki Beach has gentle waves and a shallow shoreline, so it's safe for kids to splash around. The Diamond Head trek is an easy enough climb for elementary-school children, and there's a range of family programs like the Polynesian Cultural Center, Sea Life Park Hawaii, and the Honolulu Zoo. As U.S. territory, it has excellent medical facilities, and with a large Korean community, Korean restaurants are easy to find. The time difference is 19 hours behind Korea, which effectively works like being 5 hours ahead, so it takes a few days to adjust.

3. Tokyo

Tokyo is the closest and most convenient family destination. With a flight time of 2.5 hours and no time difference, the burden is minimal. Tokyo Disneyland and DisneySea are world-famous theme parks that thrill kids of every age. Ueno Zoo, teamLab Borderless (a digital art museum), KidZania Tokyo, and Legoland Tokyo are also popular with children. Japan's meticulous hygiene management and safe streets make it ideal for family travel, and you can easily pick up kids' snacks, formula, and diapers at convenience stores and supermarkets. Public transit is punctual and convenient, and getting around with a stroller is hassle-free.

Tokyo family travel tip: Tokyo Disneyland has far shorter wait times if you visit on a weekday. Using the paid "Premier Access" fast-pass also lets you ride the popular attractions before your child gets worn out. Keep in mind, too, that admission is free for children under 3.

4. Bali

Bali is a family destination where you can experience nature and culture at the same time. With about 7 hours of flight time and a 1-hour time difference, it offers great value thanks to low costs. If you stay at a resort with a kids' club, parents can take a break for a while as professional staff look after the children. There's a wealth of activities you can enjoy with kids—the Ubud Monkey Forest, Bali Safari Park, Waterbom Bali (water park), and Bali Bike Park. That said, traffic in central Bali is heavy and hygiene varies widely from place to place, so you'll want to be careful about choosing accommodation and restaurants. Always boil tap water before drinking it or buy bottled water.

5. Sydney

Sydney is a place where you can show your child the wonders of the great outdoors. It's a long haul at about 10 hours of flight time, but with only a 1-hour time difference (2 hours during daylight saving), there's hardly any jet lag to adjust to. Bondi Beach and Manly Beach are family-friendly, and at Taronga Zoo you can see koalas and kangaroos up close. There are plenty of great spots for families, including SEA LIFE Sydney Aquarium, Blue Mountains National Park, and the Powerhouse Museum. Australia has excellent hygiene and safety, and with English as the common language, communication is easy. Since the seasons are the opposite of Korea's, you also get the advantage of enjoying a warm summer in Sydney while it's winter back home.

sections.h2: Flight Tips: A Survival Guide to Long-Haul Flights with Kids
sections.html:
Flying with kids is the biggest worry for many parents—if your child cries or fusses on board, it's hard on you and you feel bad for the passengers around you. But with the right preparation, you can make the flight go far more smoothly.

Choosing seats

Bulkhead seats (the first row, with a wall in front) are the most recommended seats for families traveling with children. There's no seat in front so you get more room, and depending on the airline, you can have an infant bassinet installed. Bassinet seats suit infants under 2 years old and under 10 kg, and since the criteria vary by airline, check when you book.

If your child loves the window seat, go for the window. They can pass the time watching the clouds and sky, and can lean against the wall to fall asleep. That said, if your child makes frequent bathroom trips, an aisle seat is more convenient. For a family of 3–4, sitting side by side in the same row rather than in front-and-back rows makes it easier to help one another.

Carry-on essentials

The most important thing on a flight with kids is something to keep your child entertained. Download their favorite movies and games onto a tablet in advance. There's an in-flight entertainment system, but it may lack content suited to young children. Bringing a new toy, a sticker book, or a coloring book can hold their attention for a while thanks to the curiosity of something they haven't seen before. For headphones, prepare a separate pair of kids' headphones sized for your child's ears.

Be ready for ear pain during takeoff and landing. If pressure changes make their ears hurt, your child may cry hard. For infants, offer a bottle or pacifier; for toddlers, giving candy or jelly helps regulate ear pressure through the swallowing motion. A blocked nose makes ear pain worse, so if your child has rhinitis or a cold before the flight, consult a pediatrician.

In-flight meal tip: Most airlines offer a special child meal (Child Meal). You can request it when booking, or up to 24–48 hours before departure via the airline's website or call center. Child meals are made up of kid-friendly items (chicken nuggets, pasta, and the like), so children eat them better than the standard in-flight meal. For infants who need baby food, you can bring the amount you need on board in line with liquid-carry-on rules.

Adjusting to jet lag

When traveling to a destination with a large time difference, helping your child adjust to jet lag is a big challenge for parents too. The most effective approach is to gradually shift their sleep schedule 2–3 days before departure. If the destination is in a time zone behind Korea's, push bedtime back by 30 minutes to an hour; if it's ahead, put them to bed earlier.

After arriving, getting plenty of daylight during the day is the key to adjusting to jet lag. Outdoor activity during the day regulates melatonin secretion, making it easier to fall asleep at night. On the first day, even if your child is tired, don't let them nap too long. A short nap of 30 minutes to an hour is fine, but if they sleep for 3 hours or more, they won't sleep at night and jet-lag adjustment gets delayed.

On a family trip, accommodation isn't just a place to sleep—it's a comfortable place for your child to rest. Whether a hotel or an Airbnb (a homestay-style rental) is better depends on your family's situation.

Hotels

The advantages of a hotel are its service and amenities. You can get help from the front desk around the clock, and the concierge can handle restaurant reservations or transportation questions. Many hotels offer family rooms or connecting rooms, so kids and parents can sleep in separate spaces. At a resort-style hotel with a pool, kids' club, or playroom, your child can have plenty of fun without even leaving the hotel.

When booking a hotel, check the family-room configuration carefully. Sleeping with your child in a room with a single double bed can be uncomfortable, so check whether twin beds or an extra bed are available. Many hotels let children under 12 use existing bedding for free, and you can request an extra bed or a crib.

Airbnb / homestay-style rentals

The biggest advantage of an Airbnb is the space and kitchen. Renting a 2- or 3-bedroom apartment gives you more room than a hotel, and you can cook familiar food for your child yourself in the kitchen. This is especially practical if you have an infant on baby food or a picky eater. If the place has a washing machine, you can wash your child's clothes as needed and cut down on how much you pack.

That said, with an Airbnb you need to check the location and safety carefully. Read plenty of reviews and choose a place that has been rated as "good for family travel." It's a good idea to ask the host in advance whether there are any elements that could be dangerous for a child—high-floor balconies, stairs without safety gates, sharp-cornered furniture, and the like.

Comparison Hotel Airbnb
Space Limited (family room needed) Spacious (2–3 bedrooms possible)
Kitchen Usually none Usually available
Service Front desk, concierge, room service Self-service
Safety Key card, CCTV, 24-hour staff Varies by host
Laundry Paid laundry service Free use of washing machine
Price (family of 4) Higher Relatively cheaper
Best for Resort getaways, short trips Long trips, independent travel

sections.h2: Adjusting Itinerary Intensity by Your Child's Age
sections.html:
The most common mistake on a family trip is cramming in too much. On an adults-only trip you can cover 4–5 places in a day, but with kids along you should cut that to less than half. When a child gets worn out, the crying and fussing begin—and in that moment, the parents wear out too. A relaxed schedule makes the whole family happy.

Ages 0–2 (infants)

Traveling with an infant realistically means a parent-centered itinerary with the child along for the ride. Plan just 1–2 main activities a day and let the rest of the time follow your child's sleep, feeding, and diaper changes. Choose places where a stroller can move easily and where nursing rooms or diaper-changing stations are available. Visiting one place in the morning, then putting the child down for a nap at the accommodation, followed by a light stroll in the late afternoon, is about right. At this age a child won't remember the trip, so prioritize managing the parents' stamina and condition.

Ages 3–5 (toddlers)

Toddlers are bursting with curiosity, but their stamina has clear limits. 2–3 activities a day is about right, and be sure to build in 30 minutes to an hour of downtime between activities. They need time to have a snack at a café or run around freely at a park. Keep the total walking distance to within 2–3 km a day, and use taxis or public transit for getting around when you can. Bringing a stroller is handy so you can put your child in it when they tire out. Zoos, aquariums, and playgrounds—places where a child can see, touch, and experience things firsthand—are ideal.

Ages 6–9 (lower-grade elementary)

Lower-grade elementary kids can handle 3–4 activities a day, and can walk up to 5–6 km a day. Activities that combine learning and play—theme parks, museums, hands-on programs—work well. Include your child's input by asking, "What do you want to do today?" They'll take part far more eagerly in activities they chose themselves. That said, fatigue builds up after around 3–4 p.m., so schedule the high-energy activities in the morning and wrap up the afternoon with something lighter.

Ages 10 and up (upper-grade elementary to middle school)

At this age they have stamina similar to an adult's and can handle 4–5 activities a day. Including activities with educational value—historic sites, art museums, local cultural experiences—can add a learning benefit too. Watching a book or video about the destination together before the trip raises their interest and understanding once you're there. You can also hand a child of this age responsibility for the travel record (taking photos, keeping a journal), which gives them a sense of responsibility and accomplishment.

A trip abroad with kids inevitably means more luggage. But leave out something truly necessary and you'll face real inconvenience on the ground. Here's a rundown of the essentials to pack, organized by age.

Shared essentials:

  • Passports (for anyone under 18, always check the validity—at least 6 months remaining)
  • Travel insurance certificate (coverage for the whole family)
  • First-aid kit: fever reducer (children's acetaminophen), anti-diarrheal, bandages, insect-bite ointment, disposable thermometer
  • Sunscreen (SPF 50+, kids' formula)
  • Tableware: child's utensils, water bottle, snack container
  • Power bank, charging cables
  • Emergency contact card (put the parents' contact info and hotel address in your child's bag)

Extras for infants and toddlers (ages 0–3):

  • Diapers (available locally, but bring plenty for the first day)
  • Wet wipes (a large supply—also useful for cleaning during the trip)
  • Baby food, formula (the same product may be hard to find locally)
  • Stroller (a lightweight folding stroller is recommended)
  • Baby carrier (Ergobaby, Konny, etc.)
  • Baby laundry detergent (for hotel laundry service)

Extras for toddlers to elementary-school age (ages 4–12):

  • Tablet + headphones (entertainment in-flight and on the move)
  • A favorite toy or stuffed animal (whatever they need at bedtime)
  • Swimsuit, rash guard
  • Light snacks (jelly, biscuits, jerky—items allowed in carry-on)
  • Travel clothesline (for drying your child's clothes after washing)
Note: Always check your child's passport validity. Many countries require at least 6 months remaining on the passport at entry. A child's passport is valid for 5 years, so it expires sooner than an adult's. Check the passport's status 3 months before departure.

sections.h2: Preparing for Emergencies: Insurance and Local Hospitals
sections.html:
The biggest worry on a trip with kids is when your child gets sick. An adult can tough out a mild ache or an upset stomach, but a child can't. It's inevitable to feel flustered when your child falls ill abroad, so preparing in advance is the key.

Family travel insurance

On a family trip, travel insurance isn't optional—it's essential. In particular, secure a sufficient medical-cost coverage limit for your child. Overseas pediatric care can cost several to several dozen times more than in Korea. In the U.S., a child's emergency-room visit runs at least the equivalent of about 2 million won, and hospitalization can be billed at several million won a day. Family travel-insurance plans apply a family discount, making them cheaper than individual policies, and your child's medical coverage applies equally.

When buying insurance, choose a plan that includes a 24-hour emergency assistance service. If your child gets sick in the middle of the night abroad, you can call the insurer's emergency line for guidance to a nearby hospital, medical interpretation, and direct-billing service.

Look up local hospital information in advance

Before you leave, research hospitals with pediatric care at your destination in advance. Saving the address and contact details of an international hospital or pediatric clinic near your hotel on your phone lets you respond quickly in an emergency. In major cities like Singapore, Tokyo, and Bangkok, there are international hospitals with interpretation available in Japanese, English, and Korean.

For pediatric visits, it helps to prepare your child's health information in English. Write a simple English memo covering any allergies, medications they're taking, past medical history, and vaccination records. Giving the doctor accurate information prevents misdiagnosis and helps your child get the right treatment.

First-aid tip: The same medications you use in Korea may be hard to find abroad, so get a first-aid supply prescribed at your pediatrician's in advance. Fever reducer (children's acetaminophen syrup), antihistamine (for allergic reactions), electrolyte supplement (to prevent dehydration), and ointment (for insect bites and cuts) are especially essential. When carrying liquids on board, they must be in containers of 100 ml or less, placed in a clear zip-top bag.

sections.h2: Building a Custom Family Itinerary with AI
sections.html:
Building a family itinerary entirely by hand takes a lot of time and effort. You have to factor in your child's age, interests, stamina, meal times, and nap times, while also checking travel routes between attractions, opening hours, and whether reservations are required. This is where myTravel's AI trip planning feature is a big help.

Enter your destination and travel dates into myTravel, and the AI analyzes recent travel trends and real traveler data to automatically generate an itinerary. Mark it as a family trip and it builds the schedule around kid-friendly places, adjusting travel distances and the intensity of the itinerary appropriately. It recommends efficient routes so your paths don't overlap, and shows the estimated time and mode of travel for each stop.

The AI-generated itinerary is fully editable. If you want to "spend the whole day at Disneyland on this day," just change that date to Disneyland. You can add or remove places, and rearrange the order. If you edit the itinerary during the trip, the change applies only to stops you haven't visited yet, so records that are already complete stay intact.

myTravel also displays local weather and time-difference information alongside your itinerary. You can get guidance like "There's a high chance of rain this day, so it may be better to add indoor activities," making it easier to adjust the plan for the weather. With the offline cache feature you can check your itinerary even when the internet cuts out, so you can use it with confidence abroad.

sections.h2: Closing: A Family Trip Doesn't Have to Be Perfect
sections.html:
The most important mindset on a family trip is that "it doesn't have to be perfect." Your child might cry, things might not go as planned, and the unexpected might happen. All of it is part of the journey, and looking back later, it becomes a precious memory.

Use the guidance in this article to prepare thoroughly on the basics, but stay flexible once you're there. If your child gets tired, trim the schedule without hesitation, and give them ample time at the places that excite them. The trip where the whole family is smiling is the most successful trip of all.

Try building a custom family itinerary with myTravel. The AI recommends places and schedules that work well with kids, and even provides local weather and time-difference information. Add a relaxed frame of mind on top of thorough preparation, and your family's most beautiful memories will come together.
